subsystems.name: Host interface
subsystems.role: connects the accelerator card to the server CPU over PCIe, or coherently over CXL.

subsystems.name: Vector memory
subsystems.role: holds the embedding database close to the compute so it is not re-fetched over the bus.

subsystems.name: Distance engines
subsystems.role: compute dot products or Euclidean distances between a query and many stored vectors in parallel.

subsystems.name: Index traversal unit
subsystems.role: walks the search structure instead of brute-forcing every vector.
parts: graph adjacency walker for HNSW-style indexes
inverted-list / centroid scanner for IVF-style indexes

subsystems.name: Quantisation and compression engine
subsystems.role: stores vectors in compressed form so more of the index fits in fast memory.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: builds the index, batches queries and keeps results accurate.
parts: integration with a vector-search library and database

buildSteps.title: Characterise the workload
buildSteps.detail: Measure embedding dimension, database size, queries per second and the recall the application actually needs; recall targets set how much compression is acceptable.

buildSteps.title: Architect the datapath
buildSteps.detail: Decide how many distance engines fit per memory channel and how the traversal unit schedules them, then model throughput and memory bandwidth in simulation.

buildSteps.title: Write and verify the RTL
buildSteps.detail: Implement the design in a hardware description language and verify it against a software reference index so that search results match bit-for-bit where required.

buildSteps.title: Emulate on FPGAs
buildSteps.detail: Run real indexes on FPGA prototypes to catch bandwidth bottlenecks before committing to silicon.

buildSteps.title: Physical design and tape-out
buildSteps.detail: Synthesise, place and route, check timing and design rules, then send the layout for mask-making at a foundry.

buildSteps.title: Package with memory
buildSteps.detail: Attach HBM stacks on a silicon interposer so the distance engines get terabyte-per-second bandwidth without leaving the package.

buildSteps.title: Bring up and test silicon
buildSteps.detail: Power on, run memory training and built-in self-test, then bin parts by speed.

buildSteps.title: Build the software stack
buildSteps.detail: Write the driver, an index format that lives in device memory, and an API that a vector database can call in place of its CPU or GPU path.

buildSteps.title: Benchmark recall versus throughput
buildSteps.detail: Compare recall@k and latency against a tuned software baseline (such as FAISS or ScaNN on a GPU) — if the accelerator does not beat it per watt, it has no market.

prerequisites.why: graph and inverted-list indexes (HNSW, IVF) are what the hardware would traverse; without them there is nothing to accelerate.
product and scalar quantisation shrink vectors so an index fits in on-package memory at acceptable recall.
distance computation is memory-bound, so HBM-class bandwidth is the whole point of a dedicated chip.
lets the CPU and accelerator share one vector index instead of copying it, which matters for databases.
putting comparison logic inside DRAM removes the bus entirely — demonstrated in research silicon but not a mass-market part for search.

pathway.milestone: vector search runs on CPUs and GPUs using libraries such as FAISS and ScaNN, with databases layering indexes on top
pathway.unlocks: working retrieval-augmented generation and semantic search at moderate scale.

pathway.milestone: FPGA and early ASIC cards that offload distance computation and index traversal
pathway.unlocks: lower latency and power per query than a general-purpose GPU for large indexes.

pathway.milestone: CXL-attached accelerators sharing a single index with the host CPU
pathway.unlocks: databases that mix filtering, joins and vector search without duplicating terabytes of embeddings.

pathway.milestone: search logic embedded in memory modules, with comparison done beside the DRAM arrays
pathway.unlocks: indexes far larger than on-package memory at near-memory bandwidth.
